questions.title: Must the scope of “similar goods/services” be consistent across different DuPont factors?
questions.question_body: The Board found under DuPont factor 2 that Apex’s “banking and financing services” are highly similar (even partially legally identical) to CC Serve’s “credit card services.” But for factor 6, it limited the relevant universe to only credit card services and excluded other banking/financing uses of ASPIRE. The Federal Circuit says that was error. Is there a doctrinal requirement that once the Board defines the parties’ goods/services as similar for factor 2, it must use the same scope when assessing third-party use/registrations under factor 6? Or is this more about avoiding an inconsistent application of the similarity standard rather than a strict rule?

questions.title: How does the TTAB interpret legacy identifications when the ID Manual entry has been deleted?
questions.question_body: The Board had to construe CC Serve’s 1998 registration for “credit card services” because that exact ID Manual entry had been deleted. It parsed the term broadly to include issuing cards, processing payments, authorization, alerts, account management, etc. What guides the TTAB’s interpretation of older identifications when the current ID Manual no longer contains that wording? Does deletion imply a narrower scope today, or does the Board default to ordinary meaning/dictionaries for the registration’s original identification?

questions.title: What counts as evidence under DuPont factor 6: actual marketplace use vs. third-party registrations?
questions.question_body: Apex submitted multiple third-party uses and registrations of ASPIRE-formative marks in financial services. The Board seemed to focus on the number of uses specifically in credit card services (nine) and treated other financial-services uses as irrelevant. On remand, how should the TTAB weigh third-party registrations compared to evidence of actual marketplace use when assessing the weakness of the ASPIRE mark? Does Federal Circuit precedent (Juice Generation, Jack Wolfskin) require actual use, or can registrations alone show conceptual weakness in a crowded field?

questions.title: Why did the Federal Circuit affirm factor 2 despite Apex not issuing credit cards?
questions.question_body: Apex is a retail bank that doesn’t offer credit cards, while CC Serve provides ASPIRE-branded credit card services with partner banks. Yet the Board (and the Federal Circuit) treated the services as highly similar and even partially legally identical. What’s the doctrinal basis for finding similarity when the applicant doesn’t currently offer the exact service (credit cards)? Is it because Apex’s ID covers broad “banking and financing services,” which can encompass extending credit via cards, so the comparison is based on the identification rather than current marketplace use?

questions.title: How does third-party use affect the first DuPont factor’s ‘commercial impression’ analysis?
questions.question_body: The court vacated the Board’s factor 1 analysis because reconsideration of factor 6 (marketplace crowding) could change the mark’s commercial strength and therefore the overall commercial impression. Mechanically, how does evidence of a crowded field (many ASPIRE-formative marks) feed into factor 1? Does it reduce the source-indicating power of the shared term and shift the analysis toward the differences (e.g., the word BANK, design elements), or is that effect formally captured under factor 6 and only indirectly influences factor 1?

questions.title: Who are the ‘relevant consumers’ under factor 6 when services are highly similar but not identical?
questions.question_body: The Board limited the relevant public to consumers of ‘credit card services’ and excluded broader banking/financing consumers. The Federal Circuit criticized that narrowing after the Board had already found the services highly similar under factor 2. When services are ‘legally identical in part’ and otherwise highly similar, how should the TTAB define the relevant consuming public for factor 6? Should it encompass the overlapping market of banking/financing consumers, or be limited to the exact identification of the opposer’s services?

questions.title: Does partnering with a bank to issue ASPIRE-branded cards qualify as offering ‘credit card services’ for Section 2(d)?
questions.question_body: CC Serve ‘joins with a bank’ and the bank issues ASPIRE-branded credit cards; CC Serve services the accounts. Apex argued CC Serve isn’t providing banking services itself. For Section 2(d) comparisons, does it matter that CC Serve isn’t a bank? Is providing and servicing an ASPIRE-branded credit card program with a bank partner still considered ‘credit card services’ such that it can conflict with an applicant’s broader ‘banking and financing services’?

questions.title: Standard of review check: Which issues were factual vs. legal in this likelihood-of-confusion appeal?
questions.question_body: The Federal Circuit reviews TTAB legal conclusions de novo and factual findings for substantial evidence. Here, it affirmed the Board’s factor 2 finding (substantial evidence), but vacated factor 6 for legal error in the scope of ‘similar goods’ and also vacated factor 1 as dependent on factor 6. Can someone parse precisely which parts of the factor 6 analysis are treated as legal vs. factual (e.g., defining the comparison scope vs. counting/assessing third-party uses), and why the Federal Circuit could vacate for legal error rather than reweighing the evidence?

questions.title: Is there a numeric threshold for third-party uses to show weakness under Juice Generation/Jack Wolfskin?
questions.question_body: The Board thought nine third-party ASPIRE-formative uses in credit card services were insufficient compared to the ‘considerable’ or ‘ubiquitous’ showings in Juice Generation and Jack Wolfskin (26 uses; numerous registrations and uses). Does Federal Circuit precedent set any rough threshold for how many third-party uses suffice to show commercial weakness? Or is the key inquiry the nature and proximity of those uses to the relevant services and consumers rather than a raw count?

questions.title: Why were ‘Costs to appellant’ awarded after an affirm-in-part/vacate-in-part outcome?
questions.question_body: The judgment line reads ‘Costs to appellant,’ even though the court affirmed the Board on factor 2 but vacated and remanded on factors 6 and 1. Under Federal Circuit Rule 39 or FRAP 39, how are costs allocated in a mixed outcome like this? What types of costs are we talking about (e.g., filing fees, transcript costs), and does ‘to appellant’ mean CC Serve must pay Apex’s taxable costs despite the partial affirmance?
